Whether this process produces accurate beliefs or merely consensus depends on how people combine private evidence with their neighbors' judgments. Two families of computational models make distinct assumptions: DeGroot models synchronously average available opinions, whereas reinforcement learning (RL) models update beliefs sequentially from neighbor-specific prediction errors. These accounts have not been directly compared in controlled social networks with repeated real-time interaction. We compared them using trial-by-trial choices from two previously published experiments involving 209 and 760 participants, respectively. Participants repeatedly revised predictions in networks differing in size and topology. We fitted unweighted and degree-weighted variants of both model families and compared them using random-effects Bayesian model selection. We then used simulations parameterized by the fitted models to assess network-level accuracy and consensus. In both datasets, a DeGroot variant had the strongest group-level model evidence, although the best-fitting rule varied across individuals. Network topology also mattered: unweighted DeGroot best explained behavior in most structures, whereas degree-weighted DeGroot was favored in the highly centralized Royal Family network. Simulations showed that DeGroot averaging generally generated more consensus than naïve sequential RL, while degree-weighted RL could achieve similar accuracy and consensus depending on the assumed information-sampling order. Topology further shaped collective outcomes: hub-dominated networks could reach high consensus despite relatively low accuracy. Whether this process produces accurate beliefs or merely consensus depends on how people combine private evidence with their neighbors' judgments. Two families of computational models make distinct assumptions: DeGroot models synchronously average available opinions, whereas reinforcement learning (RL) models update beliefs sequentially from neighbor-specific prediction errors. These accounts have not been directly compared in controlled social networks with repeated real-time interaction. We compared them using trial-by-trial choices from two previously published experiments involving 209 and 760 participants, respectively. Participants repeatedly revised predictions in networks differing in size and topology. We fitted unweighted and degree-weighted variants of both model families and compared them using random-effects Bayesian model selection. We then used simulations parameterized by the fitted models to assess network-level accuracy and consensus. In both datasets, a DeGroot variant had the strongest group-level model evidence, although the best-fitting rule varied across individuals. Network topology also mattered: unweighted DeGroot best explained behavior in most structures, whereas degree-weighted DeGroot was favored in the highly centralized Royal Family network. Simulations showed that DeGroot averaging generally generated more consensus than naïve sequential RL, while degree-weighted RL could achieve similar accuracy and consensus depending on the assumed information-sampling order. Topology further shaped collective outcomes: hub-dominated networks could reach high consensus despite relatively low accuracy. Exploratory simulations showed that increasing network size improved accuracy but reduced consensus, whereas increasing average degree improved both. These findings establish DeGroot averaging as a robust baseline account of belief updating in interactive networks and show how learning rules, sampling order, and topology jointly determine whether networks become accurate, consensual, or both.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7498039\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.30693/smj.2022.11.5.82\", \"title\": [\"Link Stability aware Reinforcement Learning based Network Path Planning\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Along with the growing popularity of 5G technology, providing flexible and personalized network services suitable for requirements of customers has also become a lucrative venture and business key for network service providers. Therefore, dynamic network provisioning is needed to help network service providers. Moreover, increasing user demand for network services meets specific requirements of users, including location, usage duration, and QoS. In this paper, a routing algorithm, which makes routing decisions using Reinforcement Learning (RL) based on the information about link stability, is proposed and called Link Stability aware Reinforcement Learning (LSRL) routing. To evaluate this algorithm, several mininet-based experiments with various network settings were conducted.
